TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT

                             REPLY TO APPLICANTS’ EXCEPTIONS
                              REGARDING DIRECT-MAIL NOTICE

TO THE HONORABLE COMMISSIONERS OF THE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF
TEXAS:
     I, Christine Thies, pro se intervenor, submit this Reply to Applicants’ Exceptions to the Proposal
for Decision (“PFD”). I respond specifically to Section D of Applicants’ Exceptions, Direct-Mail
Notice of Application (FOFs 38–43; COL 10).

I. Introduction

    Applicants ask the Commission to reject the PFD’s findings concerning direct-mail notice and
replace them with findings that they used current county tax rolls, promptly provided supplemental
notice, and complied with 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3). The Honey Ridge record supports the PFD’s
findings, not Applicants’ proposed replacements.

    My notice issue was not simply the result of a recent ownership change that had not yet appeared in
county records. My notice issue was a result of using an out-of-date Bell CAD GIS parcel layer and an
older ownership file.

    Honey Ridge subdivision had been platted since 2024, and Brandon Whatley Homes LLC acquired
the property from BWH Holdings LLC – Series 2 in April 2025. Yet Applicants’ notice process relied
on the older tract and ownership information, and their mapping did not show the subdivision or its
individual parcels. Before mailing notice to me on June 1, 2026, Applicants received multiple docket
filings identifying my property, Honey Ridge, and the mapping issue.



SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349; PUC Docket No. 59475                                            Page 1
     The PFD found that Applicants did not use the county tax rolls current as of the March 26 filing
date, that more than three dozen directly affected landowners did not receive timely application notice,
and that the Thieses and several other landowners were not mailed notice until approximately 67 days
after the Application was filed. Applicants now ask the Commission to replace those findings with
language stating that supplemental notice was “promptly” provided. The record does not support that
characterization.

II. Reply to Section D.1: The record supports the PDF’s finding that the notice data was not
current

     Applicants argue that “current county tax rolls” is undefined and that no evidence establishes that
the data they used was not current.1 But the PFD did not rely on speculation alone. It relied on
Applicants’ own discovery responses, admitted exhibits, and hearing testimony.

     First, the PFD states that Applicants began collecting property-owner and address data on
December 8, 2025, and used those pulls for notices mailed March 26, 2026. For Bell County, the stated
pull dates were January 7- February 23, 2026.2 The PFD also cites evidence that other underlying
property data was assembled over earlier timeframes and that a Bell County representative told
Applicants’ contractor that Bell County mapping is updated continuously.3

     Second, the Honey Ridge evidence shows why the age and source of the data mattered. Brandon
Whatley Homes LLC purchased the platted property from BWH Holdings LLC – Series 2 on April 16,
2025.4 Yet the application notice list used the older BWH Holdings LLC – Series 2 ownership for the
tract. At the hearing, Applicants’ witness Brenda Perkins agreed that the deed history showed the April
16, 2025 sale and also agreed that Applicants had noticed BWH Holdings LLC – Series 2 rather than
Brandon Whatley Homes LLC.5

     That is important because it is not a March 2026 deed recorded days before the Application. The
ownership change from BWH Holdings LLC – Series 2 to Brandon Whatley Homes LLC occurred in
April 2025—about eleven months before the March 26, 2026 Application. The Honey Ridge
subdivision itself had been platted in 2024. The PFD cites testimony that the 35-lot subdivision filed its

 plat in September 2024, home construction began in October 2024, and Applicants’ mapping did not
identify the platted neighborhood and left 17 lots unrepresented.6

     Applicants’ Exceptions emphasize that a county’s “mapping” being updated continuously is not
the same thing as ownership records being updated continuously.7 For Honey Ridge, however, that
distinction does not help Applicants. My notice problem involved both parcel-level geography/GIS
data and ownership.8 The old parent tract remained in Applicants’ mapping even after the property
had been subdivided, and the notice was directed using an older owner.9 The record therefore provides
a concrete example of why the PFD questioned whether Applicants’ source data was current.

III. Reply to Section D.2: The cure provision does not make the June 1 notice “prompt”

     Applicants next argue that the PFD’s interpretation of Rule 22.52(a)(3)(F) makes the cure
provision meaningless. They state that, once they discovered certain landowners had not received
notice, they “immediately” notified the Commission and provided supplemental notice.10 Their
proposed Replacement FOF 39 would state that Applicants “promptly provided supplemental
notice.”11

     The issue in my case is not whether a cure provision exists. The issue is when the notice problem
became identifiable. The record shows that Applicants had specific information concerning Honey
Ridge well before June 1 via Interchange postings under Docket 59475:

     April 27, 2026: Thomas Thies and I filed our requests to intervene concerning Link B22.
     Applicants cite those filings in their Exceptions.12 The Intervenor submittal contained a map
     showing the need to add Honey Ridge.13

     May 13, 2026: I filed direct testimony. Brandon Whatley and BWH Holdings also filed testimony
     addressing Honey Ridge, its ownership history, subdivision, and mapping.14

      May 15, 2026: I filed a Draft Map Correction Notice identifying that Honey Ridge was missing
     from Applicants’ mapping.15

     June 1, 2026: Applicants mailed supplemental direct notice to Christine and Thomas Thies and
     Robert and Allison Hunsaker, along with others.16

     June 8, 2026: The Hearing on the Merits began, only seven days after the supplemental mailing.

     Applicants’ own Exceptions confirm the above filings to show that I was active in the process and
participating before June 1.17 Those same filings also matter for the cure issue: they were in the docket
and gave Applicants information about the very landowner, property, and subdivision parcels that had
been omitted. Applicants cannot rely on my pre-June 1 filings to prove I knew about the case
while treating those filings as irrelevant to when they had reason to identify and correct the
notice problem.

     The PFD’s treatment of Rule 22.52(a)(3)(F) is also narrower than Applicants suggest. The PFD
did not say the cure provision never applies. It concluded that the provision addresses an individually
missed owner and does not transform a broader front-end failure to build the mailing list from current
rolls into compliance.18 In this docket, the PFD found a pattern affecting over three dozen directly
affected landowners. That factual finding should not be replaced with a blanket statement that the later
notices were prompt.

IV. Reply to Section D.3: My independent participation does not prove compliance.

     Applicants devote substantial attention to my participation. They stated that I had actual notice,
intervened, served discovery, filed direct testimony, and filed a post-hearing brief, and therefore was
not denied an opportunity to be heard.19 I do not dispute that I participated. I dispute what Applicants
ask the Commission to infer from it.

     I found the proceeding independently. My participation did not result from Applicants’ March 26
direct-mail notice. Applicants did not mail my formal notice until June 1. The fact that I independently

 found the docket and then worked to protect my interests does not establish that Applicants complied
with the direct-mail requirement that applies to them.

     More importantly, participation and compliance are separate questions. Rule 22.52(a)(3)(F) itself
states that lack of actual notice to an individual landowner will not “in and of itself” establish
noncompliance. The PFD did not rely on my lack of notice “in and of itself.” It relied on the
underlying data, the pattern of late-noticed landowners, and the evidence showing that the current-roll
requirement was not met.20 My independent participation does not erase that record.

     Applicants’ own chart also shows why actual participation is an unreliable substitute for required
notice. Robert and Allison Hunsaker—another Honey Ridge household—were mailed supplemental
notice on June 1 and did not participate.21 A landowner who does not independently discover a case
cannot participate in deadlines and proceedings that have already passed or are about to occur.

V. Reply to Section D.4: The Commission should not rewrite the notice findings.

     Applicants argue that denial is not a permissible remedy for notice defects.22 The PFD, however,
recommends denial on independent grounds: it concludes Applicants failed to establish that the
Projects are necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public, and
separately finds notice violations.23

     My Reply is limited to the direct-mail notice issue. On that issue, the Commission does not need
to accept Applicants’ proposed rewrite of FOFs 38–43 and COL 10. Applicants’ proposed
Replacement FOF 38 would affirmatively find that they relied on “current county property tax rolls,”
and Replacement FOF 39 would find that supplemental notice was “promptly” provided. Replacement
FOF 41 would further state that no directly affected landowner entitled to notice failed to receive it
except the Edwards.24 Those proposed findings do not fairly reflect the Honey Ridge record or the
PFD’s evidentiary findings.

     The stronger course is to retain the PFD’s findings based on the admitted record. At a minimum,
the Commission should not characterize my June 1 supplemental notice as “prompt” without

 accounting for the earlier record evidence identifying Honey Ridge, its parcels, its ownership history,
and the mapping omission.

VI. Conclusion

     I respectfully ask the Commission to overrule Applicants’ exceptions to the PFD’s direct-mail
notice findings, reject Applicants’ proposed Replacement FOFs 38–41 and Replacement COL 10, and
retain the PFD’s findings concerning the use of non-current notice data and delayed notice. I also ask
the Commission not to treat my independent discovery and participation as proof that Applicants
satisfied their direct-mail notice obligation.

     The record shows more than a missed mailing to one landowner. It shows that Honey Ridge had
been platted since 2024; Brandon Whatley Homes LLC acquired the platted property in April 2025;
Applicants nevertheless used the older parent tract and owner in their notice process; and Applicants
received multiple docket filings identifying the missing Honey Ridge parcels before mailing
supplemental notice on June 1. That evidence supports the PFD and does not support Applicants’
proposed finding that the notice was promptly cured.

     For these reasons, I respectfully request that the Commission adopt the PFD’s recommendation for
denial.




Respectfully submitted,




Christine Thies
